rationale: B wins because it keeps the dangerous holes visible instead of decorating them, especially in "whether the exam itself contributes revenue — which the company explicitly has NOT broken out." A has the strongest extra lens with "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete. Instead it's opening 40 more," but it also lets the rhetoric outrun the supplied facts. This is close; B is simply the set I'd trust more in a founder's hands before a reporter starts pulling threads.
gaps_in_A: "Warby Parker was supposed to make optical stores obsolete" is a great headline, but the prompt did not supply Warby's founding premise. Use it only if the founder can back it with public history or a company source.

"Warby Parker's retail expansion means a large new employer of optometrists" overstates scale and employment model before proving how many optometrists are needed or whether they are employed, contracted, or subleased.
"primary care delivery" is too broad for optometrist-staffed eye exams. Retail health, routine care, or vision care are safer; primary care invites a reporter to swat it down.
The pharmacy angle says "healthcare access" and "optical care," but the fact supplied is only glasses sales through a national pharmacy chain. No exams or care pathway yet.
gaps_in_B: "LensCrafters, EssilorLuxottica, Pearle Vision, and the big-box optical chains" are plausible category references, but they are not in the update. Fine as reporter-orientation, not as evidence.
"the historically defensible, insurance-tied part of the optical business the incumbents have owned" needs proof. It sounds smart, which is exactly why it can become unsupported analyst cosplay.

"The store that costs more to build is the one Warby says pays off" assumes the cost structure before the prompt gives capex or store-level economics. The proof section partly fixes it, but the headline is ahead of the record.
B misses A's optometry-workforce lens. That is a real trade angle if the staffing model and market-by-market hiring needs can be proved.
